title: Taiwan’s Tech Hurdles Threaten Military Capability and Potential Coalition Defense
gist: Chao and Bresnick review every Mandarin-language AI article published since 2023 by Taiwan's military journals and INDSR — roughly 50 versus nearly 90 on unmanned systems — and find six self-identified barriers to military AI: fragmented governance, weak digital infrastructure and cloud capacity, an underdeveloped data enterprise, air-gapping versus AI integration tension, weak civil-military collaboration, and an AI talent gap in a force only ~80 percent manned. They argue Taiwan's chip leadership does not translate into military AI capability, and that the May 2026 special defense budget — which funded U.S. arms purchases while cutting domestic emerging technology programs — shows why AI must move into the annual budget process.

themes.theme: Chip Leadership Does Not Equal Military AI

insights.claim: Taiwan produces the world's most advanced semiconductors yet its own military is only in the opening stages of adopting artificial intelligence systems, a mismatch that bears directly on its ability to deter Chinese aggression.
insights.speaker: Fanny Chao and Sam Bresnick
insights.so_what: Semiconductor dominance is not a defense asset in itself — a caution against reading TSMC's position as strategic security for the island.
insights.locator: Taiwan produces the world’s most advanced semiconductors

insights.claim: Fielding military AI depends less on making advanced chips, which Taiwan excels at, than on innovating defense software, building robust data pipelines, and integrating models — areas where Taipei has underinvested.
insights.speaker: Fanny Chao and Sam Bresnick
insights.so_what: Identifies where defense-tech spending and partnership demand will actually land in Taiwan: software and data infrastructure, not silicon.
insights.quote: Fielding military AI depends less on making advanced chips, a task at which Taiwan excels, than on innovating defense software, creating robust data pipelines, and integrating models, which are areas where Taipei has underinvested.
insights.locator: Fielding military AI depends less on making advanced chips

insights.claim: The Taiwanese military could be the first force to contend with the People's Liberation Army's emerging AI-enabled defense technologies in a potential conflict, given Beijing's focus on reunification.
insights.speaker: Fanny Chao and Sam Bresnick
insights.so_what: Taiwan is the first live test of AI-enabled combat power — the outcome would reset defense-tech valuations globally.
insights.locator: Beijing is pushing to develop and field sophisticated AI-enabled military capabilities.

themes.theme: Evidence Base: What Taiwan's Own Analysts Publish

insights.claim: A review of all open-source Mandarin-language AI articles published since 2023 by Taiwan's military journals and the Institute for National Defense and Security Research found nearly 50 AI articles, of which only about one-third address the AI problems Taiwan faces.
insights.speaker: Fanny Chao and Sam Bresnick
entities: Institute for National Defense and Security Research
insights.so_what: The domestic analytical base on military AI is thin, which slows the internal advocacy needed to move budgets.
insights.locator: We reviewed all of the AI-focused, open-source, Mandarin-language articles

insights.claim: The same Taiwanese journals and think tank published nearly 90 articles on unmanned systems over the same period versus roughly 50 on AI, indicating AI is comparatively under-discussed in Taiwan's defense community.
insights.speaker: Fanny Chao and Sam Bresnick
insights.so_what: Attention and therefore procurement momentum in Taiwan sits with drones, not AI software — relevant to which vendors get traction.
insights.locator: AI still appears to be a relatively under-discussed topic

insights.claim: Taiwan's defense community has identified six barriers to military AI: governance, digital infrastructure, the data enterprise, cybersecurity, military-civil collaboration, and AI talent.
insights.speaker: Fanny Chao and Sam Bresnick
insights.so_what: A six-part diagnostic checklist usable to score any military's AI readiness, not just Taiwan's.
insights.locator: Taiwan’s defense community has identified six barriers

insights.claim: Taiwanese defense authors seldom offer broader diagnoses of institutional, infrastructural, and operational barriers to military-wide AI operationalization, unlike U.S. experts whose debates cover procurement cycles and inflexible funding restrictions.
insights.speaker: Fanny Chao and Sam Bresnick
insights.so_what: The absence of systemic critique inside Taiwan suggests reform pressure will have to come from budget politics or foreign partners.

themes.theme: Fragmented Governance and the Time Constraint

insights.claim: Taiwan's Ministry of National Defense has established neither a unified AI framework nor common technical standards, organizing military AI interests around specific use cases rather than coherent technical or operational architectures.
insights.speaker: Fanny Chao and Sam Bresnick
insights.so_what: Use-case-first adoption produces duplicated spending and unintegrable systems — the pattern to watch for in any defense AI program.
insights.locator: They argue that the Ministry of National Defense has established neither

insights.claim: Fragmented development might eventually succeed given a long enough timeline, but Taiwan does not have that luxury — stovepiped development, internal competition, and eventual consolidation could consume years the island may not have.
insights.speaker: Fanny Chao and Sam Bresnick
insights.so_what: Time, not money or technology, is the binding constraint on Taiwanese military modernization.
insights.locator: Skeptics could argue that a more fragmented development pathway

insights.claim: AI systems developed under siloed Taiwanese governance structures would have limited inter-service interoperability in a near-term conflict and would be harder to integrate with partner militaries' AI tools.
insights.speaker: Fanny Chao and Sam Bresnick
insights.so_what: Governance fragmentation today directly degrades coalition combat effectiveness later — a second-order cost rarely priced into defense planning.

insights.claim: Since 2024 Taiwan's Ministry of National Defense has established a Defense Innovation Office and a dedicated AI office focused on accelerating acquisition of applications such as image recognition and cyber defense, and has stated its intention to create an AI Governance Committee for risk classification, development verification, and security monitoring.
insights.speaker: Fanny Chao and Sam Bresnick
insights.so_what: Concrete institutional entry points for defense-tech vendors seeking Taiwanese contracts.
insights.locator: Since 2024, it has established the Defense Innovation Office

insights.claim: Taiwan's Ministry of National Defense is struggling to make sufficient investments in basic digital equipment and has established only limited network bandwidth in remote areas, creating difficulties in ensuring reliable communications.
insights.speaker: Fanny Chao and Sam Bresnick
insights.so_what: Basic connectivity gaps mean AI tools would fail exactly where dispersed defense doctrine needs them most.

insights.speaker: Fanny Chao and Sam Bresnick

insights.claim: Creating military data-sharing standards will require Taipei to redress domestic technical and legal barriers, and legal changes enabling cross-border military data sharing would reduce barriers to fighting alongside the United States.
insights.speaker: Fanny Chao and Sam Bresnick

insights.claim: Taiwan's protective approach of strict hardware controls and air-gapping is hardly compatible with software-intensive AI systems requiring frequent updates and widespread data access, forcing an explicit tradeoff between cybersecurity and operational utility.
insights.speaker: Fanny Chao and Sam Bresnick
insights.so_what: A structural contradiction with no clean fix — a durable ceiling on how fast any highly penetrated military can adopt AI.

insights.claim: Air-gapping is defensible because Taiwan is constantly targeted by Chinese intelligence and Taiwanese military personnel have leaked information to Beijing, but declining to build a smoother system for pooling AI data could be equally risky.

insights.so_what: Insider-threat reality is the reason Taiwan cannot simply copy US data architectures — a permanent handicap in coalition integration.

insights.claim: Shifting toward software-based cyber defenses and shared standards would require not only significant Taiwanese cyber policy changes but a willingness to experiment with novel cybersecurity approaches.

insights.claim: The Taiwanese military has filled only around 80 percent of its total positions, and soldiers are already busy countering China's daily coercive activities alongside heightened training and normal duties.

insights.so_what: A 20 percent manning shortfall plus grey-zone operational tempo leaves no slack for the retraining AI adoption requires.

insights.claim: A limited number of technically proficient personnel could make Taiwanese AI systems superficial technology displays rather than useful battlefield tools, and poor training could lead to misinterpretation of AI outputs in a contingency.

insights.claim: The difficulty of building interoperable AI systems, as evidenced by AUKUS and NATO, stems partly from fragmentation of governance frameworks, security and technical standards, computer networks, and data — so Taiwan's gaps are also future coalition weaknesses.
